intro: Nine matriculation-exam-style problems bring together the magnetism, induction and light of the lesson. The seventh problem is an applied source-based problem whose source material is behind the link in the problem. Solve them as in the exam: name the phenomenon and the model and justify why the model fits the situation, solve for the unknown before substituting numbers, and assess whether the result is reasonable. Open the model answer and the marking scheme only when your solution is ready.

tasks.title: Electricity from a small hydropower plant
tasks.source_note: The power plant and the numbers are an invented example. A real generator has several coils and pole pairs; here a one-coil model is used.
tasks.text:
An old small hydropower plant is being renovated. A water turbine drives a generator, which is examined in a simple model: one coil rotates steadily in a uniform magnetic field. The electricity of the plant is transmitted through a transformer along a $20.0\,\text{kV}$ line $12\,\text{km}$ long to a village.

- the coil has $60$ turns and an area of $0.060\,\text{m}^2$
- magnetic flux density $0.50\,\text{T}$, rotation frequency $50\,\text{Hz}$
- transmitted power $150\,\text{kW}$, total resistance of the line's conductors $6.0\,\Omega$
- the transformer is ideal

parts.text: What is the peak value of the generator's voltage? What is its rms value?
hints: What makes the magnetic flux through the coil change as it rotates? When is the voltage at its greatest?
The peak value of the voltage of a rotating coil is $e_0 = NBA \cdot 2\pi f$, and the rms value $U$ is the direct voltage that gives the same average power.

First calculate the peak value $e_0$ from the magnetic flux density $B$, the area $A$, the number of turns $N$ and the angular frequency $2\pi f$. For a sinusoidal voltage the rms value is the peak value divided by $\sqrt{2}$.

criteria.text: Justifies that the flux through the coil changes periodically, and the voltage is at its peak when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field; the rms value is the direct voltage that gives the same average power.

criteria.detail: $e_0 = NBA \cdot 2\pi f$ and $U = \dfrac{e_0}{\sqrt{2}}$
$e_0 \approx 570\,\text{V}$ and $U \approx 400\,\text{V}$ to two significant figures like $0.50\,\text{T}$ and $0.060\,\text{m}^2$

parts.text: The generator's rms voltage $400\,\text{V}$ is stepped up with a transformer to the line voltage. What is the ratio of the numbers of turns of the transformer's secondary and primary coils? How large are the currents on each side of the transformer?
hints: What stays the same in an ideal transformer when the voltage increases? How does that affect the current?
The turns ratio is $\dfrac{N_2}{N_1} = \dfrac{U_2}{U_1}$. In an ideal transformer power is conserved, so on each side the current is $I = \dfrac{P}{U}$.

The primary voltage is the generator's $400\,\text{V}$ and the secondary voltage is the line's $20.0\,\text{kV}$. Convert kilovolts to volts and the power $150\,\text{kW}$ to watts, and calculate the currents separately on each side.

criteria.text: Justifies that in an ideal transformer the ratio of the voltages is the ratio of the turns and power is conserved, so the current decreases in the same ratio as the voltage increases.

criteria.detail: $\dfrac{N_2}{N_1} = \dfrac{U_2}{U_1}$ and $I = \dfrac{P}{U}$ on each side
$N_2 : N_1 = 50$, $I_1 \approx 375\,\text{A}$ and $I_2 \approx 7.50\,\text{A}$

parts.text: What fraction of the transmitted power is converted into internal energy in the line? What would happen if the same power were transmitted along the same line directly at the generator voltage $400\,\text{V}$?
hints: What current flows in the line? Where does the electrical energy go in the conductors of the line?
The power loss in the conductors of the line is $P_\text{h} = RI^2$, where $I$ is the current in the line. The fraction of the transmitted power lost is $\dfrac{P_\text{h}}{P}$.

Use the high-voltage current from part b and calculate the power loss in watts. Divide it by the transmitted power $150\,\text{kW}$ (convert to watts) and give the fraction as a percentage. Then calculate the same loss with the current that would flow at $400\,\text{V}$ and consider whether the result is possible.

criteria.detail: $P_\text{h} = RI^2$, where $I = \dfrac{P}{U}$, and the fraction $\dfrac{P_\text{h}}{P}$
$P_\text{h} = 6.0\,\Omega \cdot (7.50\,\text{A})^2 \approx 340\,\text{W}$, so the fraction is $\dfrac{338\,\text{W}}{150\,000\,\text{W}} \approx 0.23\,\%$

At the voltage $400\,\text{V}$ the current would be $375\,\text{A}$ and the expression $RI^2$ would give $844\,\text{kW}$, more than the whole power: already the voltage drop $RI = 2250\,\text{V}$ would be larger than $400\,\text{V}$, so the transmission would not work at all.
The fraction $0.23\,\%$ to two significant figures like the resistance $6.0\,\Omega$

parts.text: A maintenance worker suggests that the direct voltage of the village's solar panels should also be connected to the same transformer, so that its voltage could also be stepped up to the line. Assess the suggestion.
hints: By which phenomenon does a transformer change a voltage? What must happen in the iron core for a voltage to appear in the secondary coil?

The induced voltage depends on the rate of change of the magnetic flux $\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$. What is the flux that a direct voltage across the primary coil produces in the core as a function of time?
What happens in the secondary coil if the flux does not change? Consider what kind of voltage a transformer needs and how a direct voltage could be turned into one.

criteria.text: Explains that the secondary voltage of a transformer is induced by the changing magnetic flux in the iron core: with direct current the flux is constant, so no voltage is induced in the secondary (except momentarily at switch-on).

criteria.detail: The suggestion does not work: the direct voltage must first be converted into an alternating voltage with an inverter, and only then can the transformer step it up.

tasks.title: An optical fibre to the island
tasks.source_note: The situation is an invented example. The refractive indices and the attenuation are of the order of an ordinary telecommunications fibre.
tasks.text:
An optical fibre is laid from the mainland to an island village along the seabed. Infrared light travelling in the core of the fibre carries data as short pulses.

- refractive index of the core $1.470$, refractive index of the cladding $1.455$
- length of the fibre $14.0\,\text{km}$, attenuation coefficient $0.22\,\text{dB/km}$
- there are four splices on the route, each attenuating $0.10\,\text{dB}$
- power of the transmitter into the fibre $2.0\,\text{mW}$
- speed of light in a vacuum $3.00 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$

parts.text: What is the smallest angle of incidence at the boundary between core and cladding for the light to stay in the core? What is then the largest allowed angle between a ray of light and the axis of the fibre?
hints: Under what condition is light totally reflected at the boundary between the core and the cladding? Which material has the greater refractive index?

For the critical angle $\sin\alpha_\text{r} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$, where $n_1$ is the refractive index of the core and $n_2$ that of the cladding. The angle of incidence is measured from the normal of the boundary.

First calculate the critical angle $\alpha_\text{r}$. Then draw the ray, the normal of the boundary and the axis of the fibre: the normal is perpendicular to the axis, so the angle of the ray to the axis and the angle of incidence add up to $90^\circ$.

criteria.text: Justifies that the light stays in the core by total internal reflection, which is possible because the refractive index of the core is larger than that of the cladding, and that the angle of incidence is measured from the normal of the boundary.

criteria.detail: $\sin\alpha_\text{r} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$ and relative to the axis $90^\circ - \alpha_\text{r}$
$\sin\alpha_\text{r} = \dfrac{1.455}{1.470} = 0.9898$, so $\alpha_\text{r} \approx 81.8^\circ$ and relative to the axis at most $8.2^\circ$
$\alpha_\text{r} \approx 81.8^\circ$ and $8.2^\circ$; or about $82^\circ$ and $8^\circ$; justification of the precision: the difference of the refractive indices is known only to two figures

parts.text: How long does a light pulse travelling along the axis of the fibre take from the mainland to the island? How much longer does a ray take whose angle to the axis of the fibre is the largest at which it still stays in the core?
hints: At what speed does light travel in the core? How are distance, speed and time related?
The speed of light in a material is $v = \dfrac{c}{n_1}$, and the time is $t = \dfrac{s}{v} = \dfrac{n_1 s}{c}$.

Convert the length of the fibre to metres: $14.0\,\text{km} = 14\,000\,\text{m}$. Draw a right triangle in which the distance along the axis is the length of the fibre $s$ and the angle of the ray to the axis is $90^\circ - \alpha_\text{r}$. How long is the path the ray travels? Calculate the time along that path.

criteria.detail: $v = \dfrac{c}{n_1}$ and $t = \dfrac{n_1 s}{c}$

criteria.text: Justifies that the steepest ray travels the distance $\dfrac{s}{\sin\alpha_\text{r}}$ along the fibre, because the angle between the ray and the axis is $90^\circ - \alpha_\text{r}$.

criteria.detail: $t = \dfrac{1.470 \cdot 14\,000\,\text{m}}{3.00 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}} \approx 68.6\,\mu\text{s}$ and $\dfrac{68.6\,\mu\text{s}}{0.9898} \approx 69.3\,\mu\text{s}$
$t \approx 68.6\,\mu\text{s}$ and the difference about $0.7\,\mu\text{s}$

parts.text: How much power reaches the receiver on the island?
hints: By how much does the power decrease in the fibre? Which parts of the route attenuate the light?
The total attenuation is $A = aL + 4 \cdot 0.10\,\text{dB}$, and in decibels $A = 10\,\text{dB} \cdot \lg\dfrac{P_0}{P}$.

First calculate the total attenuation $A$ in decibels. Then solve the received power $P$: write the equation as $\lg\dfrac{P_0}{P} = \dfrac{A}{10\,\text{dB}}$ and remove the logarithm with a power of ten.

criteria.detail: $A = aL + 4 \cdot 0.10\,\text{dB}$ and $A = 10\,\text{dB} \cdot \lg \dfrac{P_0}{P}$, so $P = P_0 \cdot 10^{-A/(10\,\text{dB})}$
$P \approx 0.90\,\text{mW}$ to two significant figures like $2.0\,\text{mW}$ and $0.22\,\text{dB/km}$
About $3\,\text{dB}$ halves the power, and $3.5\,\text{dB}$ leaves a little under half, $45\,\%$.

parts.text: Explain why the light stays in the fibre although the fibre bends gently with the shape of the seabed, but leaks out if the fibre is bent into a sharp turn.
hints: What happens to a ray of light at the boundary when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle? What happens when it is smaller?
Total internal reflection occurs when $\alpha > \alpha_\text{r}$, where $\sin\alpha_\text{r} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}$.
Draw a ray in a gentle and in a sharp bend. How does the angle of incidence to the normal of the boundary change as the bend gets sharper? What does this mean for bending the cable?

criteria.text: Explains that in a gentle curve the angle of incidence of the ray at the boundary stays larger than the critical angle, but in a sharp bend the ray hits the boundary on the outer side of the curve more steeply, the angle of incidence falls below the critical angle and the light refracts into the cladding.

criteria.detail: For the fibre to keep guiding light, the angle of incidence must everywhere be at least $81.8^\circ$; that is why the bending radius of the cable has a lower limit.

tasks.title: The magnetic field of a straight wire
tasks.source_note: The data are an invented example: the numbers are calculated from the model of a long straight wire with $I = 12.0\,\text{A}$, and a constant field of about $11\,\mu\text{T}$ and scatter like that of readings have been added to them.
tasks.text:
Students investigated the magnetic field of a straight wire. A direct current of $12.0\,\text{A}$ flowed in a vertical wire $2.0\,\text{m}$ long. A magnetic field sensor was placed at the height of the middle of the wire so that it measured the component along the field circling the wire. The orientation of the sensor was kept the same, and its distance $r$ from the central axis of the wire was changed. The sensor was not zeroed before the measurement.

| $r\ (\text{cm})$ | $B\ (\mu\text{T})$ |
|---|---|
| $2.0$ | $132$ |
| $3.0$ | $90$ |
| $4.0$ | $72$ |
| $6.0$ | $50$ |
| $8.0$ | $41$ |
| $12.0$ | $31$ |

parts.text: Present the magnetic flux density as a function of distance in a graph. Is the magnetic flux density inversely proportional to the distance? Justify with the data.
hints: What kind of curve would the points form if doubling the distance halved the field? What do the numbers of the table tell you?
If $B$ is inversely proportional to the distance $r$, their product $Br$ is constant.
Plot the points with both axes starting from zero, and do not join the points with a line. Calculate the product $Br$ for every row of the table and compare the products.

criteria.detail: $r\ (\text{cm})$ on the horizontal axis, $B\ (\mu\text{T})$ on the vertical axis; the axes start from zero.
Six points from the table; the points are not joined into a broken line.

criteria.text: Justifies with the data: the field decreases ever more slowly, but doubling the distance does not halve it, for example $2.0\,\text{cm} \to 4.0\,\text{cm}$ gives $132\,\mu\text{T} \to 72\,\mu\text{T}$. The product $Br$ grows from $264$ to $372\,\mu\text{T} \cdot \text{cm}$, so $B$ is not inversely proportional to the distance.

parts.text: Present the data so that a straight line fits the points. Justify your choice and fit a straight line to the points.
hints: Against which quantity should $B$ be plotted so that a straight line fits the points? How does the field depend on the distance according to theory?
The field of a long straight conductor is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi} \cdot \dfrac{1}{r}$, so $B$ is linear in $\dfrac{1}{r}$.

Convert the distances to metres and calculate $\dfrac{1}{r}$ for every row of the table in $\dfrac{1}{\text{m}}$. Plot $B$ as a function of $\dfrac{1}{r}$ and fit one line through the points. The line is not forced through the origin.

criteria.text: Justifies the linearisation: the field of a long straight wire is $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi} \cdot \dfrac{1}{r}$, so $B$ is linear in the reciprocal of the distance $\dfrac{1}{r}$, and a possible constant field only shifts the line.

criteria.detail: $\dfrac{1}{r}$ for each distance in the unit $\tfrac{1}{\text{m}}$, for example $\dfrac{1}{0.020\,\text{m}} = 50\,\tfrac{1}{\text{m}}$.
One straight line between the points; $\tfrac{1}{r}\ (\tfrac{1}{\text{m}})$ on the horizontal axis, $B\ (\mu\text{T})$ on the vertical axis. The line is not forced through the origin.

parts.text: Determine the vacuum permeability $\mu_0$ from the graph. Compare the result with the table value $4\pi \cdot 10^{-7}\,\tfrac{\text{Vs}}{\text{Am}}$.
hints: What quantity does the slope of the line represent when $\dfrac{1}{r}$ is on the horizontal axis?
The slope of the line is $k = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}$. Solve $\mu_0$ from it in symbols.

Read the slope $k = \dfrac{\Delta B}{\Delta(1/r)}$ from two points of the fitted line far apart. Convert $\mu\text{T}$ to tesla: $1\,\mu\text{T} = 10^{-6}\,\text{T}$. Compare the result with the table value by calculating the percentage difference.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(5.0\,\tfrac{1}{\text{m}};\ 23\,\mu\text{T})$ and $(50\,\tfrac{1}{\text{m}};\ 132\,\mu\text{T})$: $k \approx 2.42\,\mu\text{T} \cdot \text{m}$.

criteria.text: Interprets the slope: $k = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi}$.

criteria.detail: $\mu_0 = \dfrac{2\pi k}{I}$
$\mu_0 \approx 1.27 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{\text{Vs}}{\text{Am}}$; results $1.22$–$1.32 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{\text{Vs}}{\text{Am}}$ are accepted.
The table value is $1.257 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\tfrac{\text{Vs}}{\text{Am}}$, so the difference is about $1\,\%$, which fits the scatter of about $1\,\mu\text{T}$ in the readings.

parts.text: The line does not pass through the origin. What does the constant term tell about the measurement? According to the model, what reading would the sensor show $50\,\text{cm}$ from the wire, and why is the result only an estimate?
hints: What would the sensor show if the conductor carried no current? What other than the conductor can affect the reading?
The equation of the line is $B = \dfrac{k}{r} + b$, where the constant term $b$ is where the line crosses the vertical axis.

Read $b$ from the graph and substitute $r = 0.50\,\text{m}$ and the slope from part c into the equation. Then consider whether $50\,\text{cm}$ is small compared with the length of the conductor, $2.0\,\text{m}$, and whether the point lies within the measured range.

criteria.text: Interprets the constant term: the line crosses the $B$ axis at about $11\,\mu\text{T}$, which is a constant field independent of the current in the wire: the component of the Earth's magnetic field in the direction of the sensor and the zero offset of the sensor, because the sensor was not zeroed. This can be checked by measuring the reading with the current switched off.

criteria.detail: $B = \dfrac{k}{r} + b$

The distance is outside the measured range, and $50\,\text{cm}$ is no longer small compared with the length of the wire $2.0\,\text{m}$, so the long-wire model gives too large a value for the field of the wire; most of the reading is the constant field.

tasks.title: Colours in a bubble, a rainbow and a CD
tasks.source_note: The situation is an invented example. The refractive indices of water and the track spacing of a CD are real values.
tasks.text:
At a summer party three kinds of colours are seen in the garden on the same afternoon. The children's soap bubbles have colourful stripes. A small rainbow is seen in the drops of the lawn sprinkler when the sun shines from behind the viewer. A CD left on the table reflects colourful arcs from sunlight. A guest claims: “All three arise in the same way: white light refracts in water or plastic, and different colours refract by different amounts.”

- refractive index of water for red light $1.331$ and for violet $1.343$
- distance between adjacent tracks of a CD $1.6\,\mu\text{m}$

parts.text: Explain how a rainbow forms. On which edge of the arc is red, and why?
hints: What happens to light when it enters a water drop and leaves it? What happens to different colours if the refractive index depends on the wavelength?
The dependence of the refractive index on the wavelength is called dispersion. The law of refraction is $n_1 \sin\alpha_1 = n_2 \sin\alpha_2$.

Compare the refractive indices of red and violet light: which is greater? Which colour is refracted more? Deduce at what angle from the antisolar point each colour leaves the drop, and which edge of the arc the red is on.

criteria.text: Explains that the light refracts into the drop, reflects from its back surface and refracts out, and that the refractive index of water depends on the wavelength (dispersion), so the colours leave the drop in different directions.

Justifies that the refractive index for red is the smallest, so red is seen at the largest angle from the antisolar point, about $42^\circ$, and violet at an angle of about $40.6^\circ$: red is on the outer edge of the arc.

criteria.detail: For the rainbow the claim is correct: the colours separate because different colours refract by different amounts in water.

parts.text: Explain how the colours of a soap bubble arise. Why does the thinnest top part of the bubble look dark just before it bursts?
hints: A bubble is a thin film. Which surfaces does the light meet, and what happens to the reflected waves when they meet?

Waves reflected from the outer and the inner surface of the film have a path difference $2nd$, where $n$ is the refractive index of the film and $d$ its thickness. The path difference and the wavelength decide which wavelengths are reinforced.
Reflection from which surface inverts the phase of the wave? What happens to the path difference $2nd$ and to the phase difference of the waves as the thickness $d$ of the film approaches zero?

criteria.text: Explains thin-film interference: the waves reflected from the outer and inner surfaces of the film have the path difference $2nd$, and the thickness determines which wavelengths are reinforced and which are weakened; the colour is a mixture of the remaining wavelengths.

Justifies the dark spot: only the reflection at the outer surface inverts the wave, so in a very thin film ($2nd \approx 0$) the reflected waves are in opposite phase and weaken each other at all wavelengths.

criteria.detail: For the bubble the claim is wrong: the colours arise from interference, not from refraction, and the colour depends on the thickness of the film.

parts.text: Explain how a CD produces colours, and calculate at which angles red ($650\,\text{nm}$) and violet ($400\,\text{nm}$) light are seen in the first order when the light falls perpendicularly on the disc. Finally assess the guest's claim as a whole.
hints: What do the dense tracks of a CD do to light? What happens to the waves reflected from many tracks?
The waves reinforce one another in the directions for which the grating equation $d\sin\theta = k\lambda$ holds, where $d$ is the spacing of the tracks and $k$ the order.

Solve $\sin\theta = \dfrac{k\lambda}{d}$ for $k = 1$. Convert the wavelengths and the spacing to metres: $1\,\text{nm} = 10^{-9}\,\text{m}$ and $1.6\,\mu\text{m} = 1.6 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\text{m}$. Which colour deviates more in a grating than in a drop? Then evaluate the claim separately for each phenomenon.

criteria.text: Explains that the closely spaced tracks act as a reflection grating: the waves reflected from adjacent tracks reinforce each other in the directions for which $d\sin\theta = k\lambda$.

criteria.detail: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{650 \cdot 10^{-9}\,\text{m}}{1.6 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\text{m}} = 0.41$, so $\theta \approx 24^\circ$; for violet $\sin\theta = 0.25$ and $\theta \approx 14.5^\circ$.

criteria.text: States that in a grating red deviates most, the opposite of a prism and a drop, which shows a different origin.

criteria.detail: The claim holds only for the rainbow. The colours of the bubble and the CD arise from interference: in the bubble between the reflections from the two surfaces of the film, in the CD between the reflections from many tracks.

tasks.title: The wavelength of a laser with a grating
tasks.source_note: The report and the measurements are an invented example: the distances are calculated from a grating with $600$ lines per millimetre and the wavelength $532\,\text{nm}$, and they are rounded to tape-measure readings.
tasks.text:
A group of students measured the wavelength of a green laser pointer. The laser, the grating and a wall acting as a screen were set in line so that the beam hit the grating and the wall perpendicularly. The grating's package said $600$ lines per millimetre. With a tape measure the group measured the distance of the grating from the wall and the distances from the central maximum to the maxima on its right.

| Measured | Value |
|---|---|
| distance of the grating from the wall $L$ | $80.0\,\text{cm}$ |
| from the central maximum to the 1st-order maximum $x_1$ | $27.0\,\text{cm}$ |
| from the central maximum to the 2nd-order maximum $x_2$ | $66.4\,\text{cm}$ |

The calculations and conclusions of the report: “At small angles $\sin\theta \approx \tfrac{x}{L}$, so $\lambda = \tfrac{d x_2}{2L} = 692\,\text{nm}$. The result is the wavelength of red light, so the stated wavelength of the laser, $532\,\text{nm}$, is wrong. We did not find the third-order maximum on the wall, so the grating is faulty.”

parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the laser from each maximum.
hints: What is the line spacing of the grating? How is the angle $\theta$ obtained from the measured distances $x$ and $L$?
The spacing is $d = \dfrac{1\,\text{mm}}{600}$, the angle comes from $\tan\theta_k = \dfrac{x_k}{L}$ and the wavelength from the grating equation $\lambda = \dfrac{d\sin\theta_k}{k}$.
Convert all distances to metres. Calculate the angle $\theta_k$ from the tangent and only then its sine; do not replace the sine by the ratio $\dfrac{x}{L}$. Calculate each order separately.

criteria.detail: $d = \dfrac{1\,\text{mm}}{600}$, $\tan\theta_k = \dfrac{x_k}{L}$ and $\lambda = \dfrac{d\sin\theta_k}{k}$

criteria.text: Justifies that the angle is calculated first from the tangent, because $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$ only at small angles, and here $\theta_2 \approx 40^\circ$.

criteria.detail: $\lambda \approx 533\,\text{nm}$ and $532\,\text{nm}$ to three significant figures like the distances

parts.text: Assess the group's conclusions.
hints: Where might the assumption in the group's calculation fail? When is the approximation $\sin\theta \approx \tan\theta$ good?
For each order compare the ratio $\dfrac{x}{L}$ used by the group with $\sin\theta$ calculated from the tangent. Which order has the greater error, and why?

Check the third conclusion: is $3\lambda < d$? With the wavelength of part a calculate $\sin\theta_3$ and the angle $\theta_3$, and then the distance $x_3 = L\tan\theta_3$. Does the maximum fit on the wall, and is it bright?

criteria.text: Shows that the mistake is in the method of calculation: the small-angle assumption gives $562\,\text{nm}$ from the $1$st order (about $6\,\%$ too much) and $692\,\text{nm}$ from the $2$nd order (about $30\,\%$ too much), because the difference grows as the angle grows.

criteria.detail: With $\Delta x \approx 0.3\,\text{cm}$ and $\Delta L \approx 0.3\,\text{cm}$, the $2$nd order gives about $530$–$535\,\text{nm}$, so the result agrees with the value $532\,\text{nm}$.

criteria.text: Calculates that the $3$rd order exists, because $3\lambda < d$: $\sin\theta_3 = 0.958$, $\theta_3 \approx 73^\circ$ and $x_3 = L\tan\theta_3 \approx 2.7\,\text{m}$, so the maximum is far away and faint, perhaps off the wall.

criteria.detail: Neither conclusion is justified: the laser is a $532\,\text{nm}$ green laser, as its colour also shows, and the grating is not faulty.

parts.text: Plan how the measurement can be improved.
hints: What is the least accurate part of the measurement? How could it be measured using two points?
How does the relative uncertainty $\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}$ change as $x$ grows? How do the uncertainties $\Delta x$ and $\Delta L$ affect the result $\lambda = \dfrac{d\sin\theta}{k}$?
How would you report the result so that it can be compared with the manufacturer's value? What else could make the measurement more reliable, and what safety rules apply when using a laser?

criteria.text: Measure the distance between the symmetric maxima $+k$ and $-k$ and halve it: measuring the gap between two points is more precise than estimating the centre of the central maximum, and the symmetry shows whether the beam is perpendicular.
Use a higher order or a larger distance $L$, so that $x$ is large and its relative uncertainty small.

criteria.detail: Estimate $\Delta x$ and $\Delta L$, calculate the wavelength with their extreme values and give the result in the form $\lambda \pm \Delta\lambda$, so that it can be compared with the manufacturer's value.

criteria.text: Repeat the measurement, preferably with readings by different people, and take care of safety: do not look into the beam, and do not point it at anyone's eyes.

tasks.title: The hospital cyclotron
tasks.source_note: The cyclotron and the numbers are an invented example. The fields and proton energies of cyclotrons producing tracers are of this order of magnitude.
tasks.text:
A hospital cyclotron accelerates protons, which are used to produce short-lived radioactive tracers for imaging. The cyclotron has two hollow D-shaped electrodes in a uniform magnetic field that is perpendicular to the path of the protons. Inside the electrodes the proton goes round half a circle at a time, and in the narrow gap between them an alternating voltage accelerates it every time it crosses the gap.

- magnetic flux density $1.20\,\text{T}$
- mass of the proton $1.673 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$ and charge $1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$
- kinetic energy of the proton when it leaves the cyclotron $8.0\,\text{MeV}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$
- peak value of the gap voltage $50\,\text{kV}$; the proton always crosses the gap when the voltage is at its peak
- the speed of the proton stays below a fifth of the speed of light, so classical mechanics is enough

parts.text: Show that the period of revolution of the proton does not depend on its speed. At what frequency must the gap voltage alternate?
hints: Which force bends the path of the proton in the magnetic field? How does it affect the speed of the proton?
The magnetic force acts as a centripetal force: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$. The period is $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v}$.

First solve the radius $r$ in symbols and substitute it into the period. Which quantity cancels? How many times must the voltage change direction during one revolution, and what frequency $f$ follows?

criteria.text: Justifies that the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and acts as the centripetal force, $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, and that the distance travelled in one revolution is $2\pi r$.

criteria.detail: $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$ and $T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m}{qB}$, from which $v$ cancels; the frequency of the voltage is $f = \dfrac{1}{T}$, because the direction changes every half revolution
$f \approx 18.3\,\text{MHz}$ to three significant figures like $1.20\,\text{T}$

parts.text: What is the speed of the proton when it comes out of the cyclotron? What is then the radius of its path?
hints: How do you get the speed of the proton from its kinetic energy? In which unit is the kinetic energy given?
The kinetic energy is $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$ and the radius of the path in the magnetic field is $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
First convert the kinetic energy to joules: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ and $1\,\text{MeV} = 10^6\,\text{eV}$. Then solve the speed $v$ and only after that the radius $r$.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_\text{k}}{m}}$, and $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$
$v \approx 3.9 \cdot 10^7\,\text{m/s}$ and $r \approx 0.34\,\text{m}$ to two significant figures like $8.0\,\text{MeV}$
$v \approx 0.13c$, so the classical model is sufficient; a diameter of about $70\,\text{cm}$ suits a hospital device.

parts.text: How many revolutions does the proton make in the cyclotron? How long does the acceleration last?
hints: Does the magnetic field or the gap accelerate the proton? How much energy does the proton gain in one crossing of the gap?
In the gap the proton gains the energy $qU$, and it crosses the gap twice per revolution. The number of revolutions is $n = \dfrac{E_\text{k}}{2qU}$ and the acceleration time $t = nT$.
The charge of the proton is the elementary charge $e$, so the energy gained in one crossing in electronvolts is the same number as the voltage in volts. Use the period $T$ from part a.

criteria.text: Justifies that only the electric field of the gap does work, $qU$ at each crossing and twice per revolution, because the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity and does not change the speed.

criteria.detail: $n = \dfrac{E_\text{k}}{2qU}$ and $t = nT$
$2qU = 2 \cdot 50\,\text{keV} = 100\,\text{keV}$, so $n = \dfrac{8.0\,\text{MeV}}{0.100\,\text{MeV}} = 80$ and $t = 80 \cdot 5.47 \cdot 10^{-8}\,\text{s} \approx 4.4\,\mu\text{s}$
$n \approx 80$ revolutions and $t \approx 4.4\,\mu\text{s}$

parts.text: What is the acceleration of the proton just before it comes out of the cyclotron? In which direction does it point?
hints: Which quantity describes the acceleration on a circular path? In which direction do the force and the acceleration point?
In circular motion the normal acceleration is $a_\text{n} = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$. It also follows from the magnetic force: $a = \dfrac{qvB}{m}$.

Use the speed and the radius of part b in SI units. In which direction does the net force point relative to the centre of the path, and what does that tell you about the direction of the acceleration?

criteria.detail: $a_\text{n} = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$ or $a = \dfrac{qvB}{m}$
$a \approx 4.5 \cdot 10^{15}\,\text{m/s}^2$ towards the centre of the path

tasks.title: How much energy is there in a particle accelerator?
tasks.source_note: CERN, The Large Hadron Collider (https://home.cern/science/accelerators/large-hadron-collider). Checked 16 Nov 2026. The figures are from the section Facts and figures of the page.
tasks.text:
The LHC (Large Hadron Collider) of CERN, the European laboratory for particle physics, is the largest particle accelerator in the world. In its ring-shaped tunnel two proton beams circulate in opposite directions in an almost perfect vacuum, and the beams are made to collide at the detectors. The protons travel in the beam in tight groups called bunches.

Open CERN's page [The Large Hadron Collider](https://home.cern/science/accelerators/large-hadron-collider) and find its section *Facts and figures*. You need information from the page in parts a and e.

According to the source (checked 16 Nov 2026):

- the energy of one proton is $6.8\,\text{TeV}$
- one proton beam has about $2500$ bunches, and each bunch contains $1.6 \cdot 10^{11}$ protons at the start of the acceleration

In addition: $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ and the speed of light in vacuum is $c = 2.99792458 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$.

parts.text: Read from the source the circumference of the LHC and how many turns the protons make per second. From these, calculate the speed of the protons and compare it with the speed of light. What can be concluded from the comparison and what cannot? Take into account the precision with which the figures of the source are given.
hints: What information do you need to calculate the speed? Find it in the *Facts and figures* section of the CERN page.
The speed is $v = \dfrac{s}{t}$. When the proton makes $N$ revolutions per second and the circumference is $l$, the distance travelled in a second is $s = Nl$.

Substitute the circumference in metres and the number of revolutions per second. Compare the speed with the speed of light with the quotient $\dfrac{v}{c}$. How many significant figures do the numbers of the source have, and what can you conclude about the difference from that?

criteria.text: Reads from the source the circumference $26\,659\,\text{m}$ and the number of turns $11\,245$ per second (checked 16 Nov 2026) and recognises that in one second the protons travel the circumference this many times.

criteria.detail: $\dfrac{v}{c} \approx 0.99996$: the protons travel at practically the speed of light. The difference is smaller than the precision of the rounded figures of the source, so its size cannot be concluded; the speed of a proton, which has mass, nevertheless stays below the speed of light.

parts.text: Convert the energy of one proton, $6.8\,\text{TeV}$, to joules.
hints: How is the electronvolt related to the joule? What does the prefix tera mean?
First write the energy in electronvolts: $6.8 \cdot 10^{12}\,\text{eV}$. Then multiply by the number that converts one electronvolt to joules.

criteria.detail: $E_1 \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^{-6}\,\text{J}$ to two significant figures like $6.8\,\text{TeV}$

parts.text: How much energy is stored in one proton beam?
hints: What does the energy of the beam consist of? What do you need to know about the number of protons?
The energy of the beam is the sum of the energies of the protons, $E = NE_1$, where $N$ is the total number of protons and $E_1$ the energy of one proton from part b.

Calculate $N$ by multiplying the number of bunches by the number of protons in a bunch: $2500 \cdot 1.6 \cdot 10^{11}$. Then multiply by $E_1$ and give the energy in megajoules: $1\,\text{MJ} = 10^6\,\text{J}$.

criteria.detail: The energy of the beam is the sum of the energies of the protons: $E = NE_1$, where $N = 2500 \cdot 1.6 \cdot 10^{11}$, that is, $N = 4.0 \cdot 10^{14}$
$E \approx 4.4 \cdot 10^8\,\text{J} = 4.4 \cdot 10^2\,\text{MJ}$ to two significant figures like $6.8\,\text{TeV}$ and $1.6 \cdot 10^{11}$

parts.text: A car has a mass of $1500\,\text{kg}$ and a speed of $100\,\text{km/h}$. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car. The energy of one proton beam corresponds to the kinetic energy of how many such cars?
hints: With which quantity do you calculate the energy of a moving car? In which unit must the speed be?
The kinetic energy is $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$. The comparison is the quotient $\dfrac{E}{E_\text{k}}$, where $E$ is the energy of the beam from part c.
Convert the speed from $\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$ by dividing by $3.6$. Calculate the kinetic energy of the car in joules and divide the energy of the beam, also in joules, by it.

criteria.detail: $\dfrac{E}{E_\text{k}} = \dfrac{4.357 \cdot 10^8\,\text{J}}{5.787 \cdot 10^5\,\text{J}} \approx 753$: the energy of one beam corresponds to the kinetic energy of about $750$ cars.

parts.text: The LHC has thousands of superconducting electromagnets. Find out from the source what the magnets do, to what temperature they are cooled and what accelerates the protons. Using this information and physics, explain why the magnetic field does not increase the energy of the protons and why the coils of the magnets are superconducting.
hints: What does the CERN page say about the task of the magnets, their temperature and what accelerates the protons? Look in the *Facts and figures* section and near it.
How much work does a force do when it is perpendicular to the direction of motion? What does that tell you about the change in the kinetic energy of the proton?
A strong magnetic field needs a large current $I$. What happens in an ordinary conductor of resistance $R$ with power $P = RI^2$, and what would change if $R$ were zero?

criteria.text: Explains what the magnets do, using the source: the magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity of the proton, so it bends the path into an arc of a circle (dipole magnets) and keeps the beam together (quadrupole magnets).

Justifies that a force perpendicular to the velocity does no work, so the magnetic field does not change the energy of the proton; the energy comes from the electric field of the accelerating cavities.
Justifies that a strong field needs a very large current and that in an ordinary conductor electrical energy would turn into internal energy at the rate $P = RI^2$.

criteria.detail: A superconductor has no resistance, so a large current flows with no power loss; that is why the coils are cooled, according to the source, to the temperature $1.9\,\text{K}$.

tasks.title: A laser experiment with an acrylic plate
tasks.source_note: The measurement and the numbers are an invented example whose points are rounded to the precision of the scale.
tasks.text: A student uses a laser pointer to study how light refracts when it goes from air into an acrylic plate. She measures the angle of incidence $\alpha_1$ in air and the angle of refraction $\alpha_2$ in acrylic at angles of incidence $10^\circ$, $20^\circ$, $\ldots$, $70^\circ$. In the graph $\sin\alpha_1$ is on the vertical axis and $\sin\alpha_2$ on the horizontal axis, and a straight line has been fitted to the data points. The refractive index of air is $1.00$, the speed of light in air is $3.00 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and the acrylic plate is $15\,\text{cm}$ thick.

parts.text: Determine the refractive index of acrylic from the graph.
hints: Which property of the line in the graph gives the refractive index? Write the law of refraction from air into acrylic.
The law of refraction is $n_1 \sin\alpha_1 = n_2 \sin\alpha_2$. In air $n_1 = 1.00$, so $\sin\alpha_1 = n\sin\alpha_2$, and $\sin\alpha_1$ is on the vertical axis.
Read two points of the fitted line that are far apart, not measured points. Calculate the slope as the quotient $\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$.

criteria.detail: The slope is read from two points far apart on the fitted line, for example $(0.30;\ 0.44)$ and $(0.60;\ 0.89)$.
Snell's law $1.00 \cdot \sin\alpha_1 = n \sin\alpha_2$, so $\sin\alpha_1 = n \sin\alpha_2$ and $n$ is the slope of the line.
$n = 1.5$ (no unit), two significant figures like the values read from the graph.

parts.text: What is the speed of light in acrylic? How long does the light take to pass through the plate when it travels perpendicular to the surface of the plate?
hints: How does the speed of light in a material depend on the refractive index? How far does light travel through the plate when it crosses perpendicularly?
The speed of light in a material is $v = \dfrac{c}{n}$ and the travel time $t = \dfrac{d}{v}$.
Use the refractive index of part a. Convert the thickness of the plate to metres: $15\,\text{cm} = 0.15\,\text{m}$. Calculate the speed $v$ first and only then the time $t$.

criteria.detail: $v = \dfrac{c}{n}$ and $t = \dfrac{d}{v}$

$$\begin{aligned}v &= \dfrac{3.00 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}}{1.5} \\&= 2.0 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}$$ and $t = \dfrac{0.15\,\text{m}}{2.0 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}} = 7.5 \cdot 10^{-10}\,\text{s}$
The thickness $15\,\text{cm}$ is converted to metres, $0.15\,\text{m}$; $v = 2.0 \cdot 10^8\,\text{m/s}$ and $t = 0.75\,\text{ns}$.

parts.text: What is the smallest angle of incidence at which total internal reflection occurs when light goes from acrylic into air?
hints: From which material into which must light travel for total internal reflection to be possible? What is the angle of refraction at the critical angle?
At the critical angle the angle of refraction is $90^\circ$, so $n\sin\alpha_\text{r} = 1.00 \cdot \sin 90^\circ$.
Solve $\sin\alpha_\text{r}$ in symbols and substitute the refractive index of part a. The angle comes from the inverse function $\arcsin$, which is $\sin^{-1}$ on a calculator.

criteria.text: Justifies that total internal reflection is possible only when light goes from an optically denser medium (acrylic, $n = 1.5$) into a less dense one (air, $n = 1.00$), and that at the critical angle the angle of refraction is $90^\circ$.

criteria.detail: $n \sin\alpha_\text{c} = 1.00 \cdot \sin 90^\circ$, so $\sin\alpha_\text{c} = \dfrac{1.00}{n}$
$\alpha_\text{c} = \arcsin\dfrac{1.00}{1.5} = 41.8^\circ$
$\alpha_\text{c} \approx 42^\circ$, two significant figures like the refractive index $1.5$.

parts.text: Why should the fitted line pass through the origin? Why is the refractive index determined from the slope of the line and not from a single data point?
hints: What happens to light when the angle of incidence is zero? What are the angles then?
What values do $\sin\alpha_1$ and $\sin\alpha_2$ take then, and through which point should the line therefore pass?

The measured points are scattered on both sides of the line. How do the quotient of a single point and the slope of the line fitted to all the data differ in how errors affect them? Does the refractive index depend on the angle of incidence?

criteria.text: Explains that when the angle of incidence is zero the light is not refracted and the angle of refraction is zero. Then $\sin\alpha_1 = 0$ and $\sin\alpha_2 = 0$, so the line must pass through the point $(0;\ 0)$. The line in the graph passes almost through the origin, so the model $\sin\alpha_1 = n \sin\alpha_2$ fits the measurement.

Explains that reading the angles of a single point has a random error, and the points are scattered on both sides of the line. The slope of a line fitted to the whole data averages the errors, so it is more reliable than the quotient $\sin\alpha_1 : \sin\alpha_2$ of one point.
States that the refractive index is a property of the material and does not depend on the angle of incidence, so all the points lie on the same line: the slope is the same for small and large angles.

tasks.title: Flux through a coil and the induced current
tasks.source_note: The coil and the numbers are an invented example.
tasks.text: A coil has $120$ turns, and its ends are connected together through a resistor so that the resistance of the whole circuit is $8.0\,\Omega$. The graph shows the magnetic flux $\Phi$ through one turn as a function of time $t$. A positive direction of the flux has been chosen, and the flux is negative when it points in the opposite direction.

parts.text: What is the voltage induced in the coil during the interval $0$–$0.40\,\text{s}$ and during the interval $0.60$–$0.80\,\text{s}$?
hints: What does the induced voltage depend on? What do you need to read from the graph?
By the law of induction, when the flux changes uniformly, $\lvert e \rvert = N\dfrac{\lvert\Delta\Phi\rvert}{\Delta t}$.

Read the value of the flux at the start and at the end of each interval from the break points of the graph and calculate the change $\Delta\Phi$. Convert $\text{mWb}$ to $\text{Wb}$. The length of the interval $\Delta t$ is read from the horizontal axis.

criteria.detail: The values of the flux are read from the turning points of the graph: $(0\,\text{s};\ 5.0\,\text{mWb})$, $(0.40\,\text{s};\ -3.0\,\text{mWb})$, $(0.60\,\text{s};\ -3.0\,\text{mWb})$ and $(0.80\,\text{s};\ 0\,\text{mWb})$.
$\lvert e \rvert = N\,\dfrac{\lvert \Delta\Phi \rvert}{\Delta t}$, because the flux changes uniformly in both intervals.
The unit $\text{mWb}$ is converted to $\text{Wb}$; $2.4\,\text{V}$ and $1.8\,\text{V}$, two significant figures like the flux values.

parts.text: How much electrical energy is converted into internal energy in the coil circuit during the whole $0.80\,\text{s}$?
hints: In which intervals does a current flow in the circuit, and in which does it not?
In the resistor electrical energy becomes internal energy. The power is $P = \dfrac{e^2}{R}$ and the energy $W = P\,\Delta t$.
Calculate the energy separately for each interval in which the voltage is not zero, using the voltages of part a. Finally add the energies together.

criteria.text: Justifies that during $0.40$–$0.60\,\text{s}$ the flux is constant, so the voltage and the current are zero and no energy is converted.

criteria.detail: $W = P\,\Delta t = \dfrac{e^2}{R}\,\Delta t$ in each interval, and the energies are added.

$$\begin{aligned}W &= \dfrac{(2.4\,\text{V})^2}{8.0\,\Omega} \cdot 0.40\,\text{s} \\&+ \dfrac{(1.8\,\text{V})^2}{8.0\,\Omega} \cdot 0.20\,\text{s} \\&= 0.72\,\text{W} \cdot 0.40\,\text{s} \\&+ 0.41\,\text{W} \cdot 0.20\,\text{s} \\&= 0.29\,\text{J} + 0.082\,\text{J} \\&\approx 0.37\,\text{J}\end{aligned}$$
$W \approx 0.37\,\text{J}$, two significant figures like the resistance $8.0\,\Omega$.

parts.text: Explain the direction of the induced current in the different intervals. How does the value zero of the flux, at the moment when the flux changes its sign, affect the current?
hints: What does Lenz's law say about the effect of the induced current on the change of the flux? In which interval is there no current at all?
By Lenz's law the magnetic field of the induced current opposes the change of the flux. In each interval work out whether the flux increases or decreases and in which direction it points.

Think about the moment when the flux is zero. Which property of the graph tells the rate of change of the flux $\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}$, and does the voltage depend on the value of the flux or on its rate of change?

criteria.text: States that a voltage is induced only when the flux changes. During $0.40$–$0.60\,\text{s}$ the flux is constant, so the voltage and the current are zero.
Applies Lenz's law in the interval $0$–$0.40\,\text{s}$: the flux decreases, so the magnetic field of the induced current points in the positive direction of the flux and opposes the decrease.

Applies Lenz's law in the interval $0.60$–$0.80\,\text{s}$: the flux increases towards zero, so the field of the induced current points in the negative direction and the current flows in the opposite direction to that in the first interval.

Concludes that at $0.25\,\text{s}$ the flux is zero but its rate of change is the same as before and after ($-20\,\text{mWb/s}$). The induced voltage depends on the rate of change of the flux and not on its value, so the voltage is $2.4\,\text{V}$ and the direction of the current does not change.
